blogs.description: Release: llm 0.37 There's a lot of stuff in this new release of my LLM CLI tool and Python library, representing around two months…
blogs.content:
Release: llm 0.37

 There's a lot of stuff in this new release of my LLM CLI tool and Python library, representing around two months of accumulated features and fixes.

 I added gpt-6.1-sol and gpt-6.1-terra , plus a new llm openai endpoint add command to make it easier to configure additional models that use OpenAI-compatible endpoints.

 I switched the default model (if you have not set your own default) to gpt-6-luna - half the price of the previous default, gpt-5.6-luna .

 LLM's support for embeddings now accepts that different binary content may have different content-type - necessary for models like Gemini Embedding 2 , which can embed text, audio, images, and video.

 A lot of open source maintainers complain about a flood of AI-assisted PRs. LLM is my project that has been most affected by this and, to be honest, I'm not finding it to be a problem. That's mainly because I have Opus 5.5 or GPT-6 Astra help me with triage to spot the most useful fixes!

 This release includes fixes from 12 authors - almost all AI-assisted - and the burden of reviewing them wasn't nearly as great as I expected. I really see them as bug reports with attached examples - sometimes I land them, sometimes I implement my own fix.

 So thanks to 0d00ciallo0721 , ac1982 , Allen Flux , Bian Yuhan , Bishop Kammeraad , Chen Yufeiyang , Christopher Krah , Ethan Stoner , Jiachen Xie , Olamide Faniyan , Sharat Chandra Sai Boddu , nosmile99 for helping out with (or spending tokens on) this release!

blogs.name: Simon Willison's Weblog
blogs.title: The U.S. Census Bureau and “Super Intelligence”
blogs.description: I was reminded today of AI Adoption Rate Trending Down for Large Companies, a chart produced by Apollo Global Management in September 2025…
blogs.content:
I was reminded today of AI Adoption Rate Trending Down for Large Companies , a chart produced by Apollo Global Management in September 2025, which appeared to show a slowdown in U.S. corporate AI adoption based on numbers collected by the U.S. Census Bureau. At the time I used that chart to demonstrate GPT-5 data analysis , and then to experiment with Claude's new Code Interpreter . I decided to try running those numbers again to see what had changed over the past year, and in doing so learned that the Bureau has fallen foul of Executive Order 14434 , aka the asinine Super Intelligence one.

 First, the updated chart

 Every two weeks the U.S. Census Bureau runs a survey called the Business Trends and Outlook Survey (aka BTOS). Each time it goes to 200,000 businesses out of 1.2 million total - the surveyed group (a "panel") cycles such that an individual business only completes the survey every twelve weeks.

 The latest data is published on alternating Thursdays at 10am.

 I used the most recent numbers (published October 22, 2026) to create a new version ( GPT-6 Astra Extra High transcript ) of the AI adoption chart, updated to reflect both the last twelve months and a change that was made to the survey question sent out by the Bureau:

 Here's a link to the larger image .

 For comparison, here's that AI adoption chart from last year (my GPT-5 version):

 In September 2025 the largest (250+ employees) companies answered "yes" around 12% of the time to the question about whether they used AI in "producing goods or services".

 Under the new "any business function" wording, by February 2026, those same large companies answered "yes" around 30% of the time, and by October 2026 that had increased to around 40%.

 The data in the above chart comes from the "Employment size class" XLSX file, available from here . Here's a copy of the file I used.

 You can view the survey document that is sent out to businesses - here's my snapshot copy of that 346KB PDF.

 The changing language of the questions

 As the chart demonstrates, the question asked by the Bureau changed in a material way on November 17th, 2025. Prior to that date, the question they asked was this (emphasis mine):

 In the last two weeks, did this business use Artificial Intelligence (AI) in producing goods or services ? (Examples of AI: machine learning, natural language processing, virtual agents, voice recognition, etc.)

 On December 3rd, 2025, the Bureau announced a significant change to that question. Here's the replacement:

 In the last two weeks, did this business use Artificial Intelligence (AI) in any of its business functions ? (Examples of AI: machine learning, natural language processing, virtual agents, voice recognition, etc.)

 No more "producing goods or services" - now it's "in any of its business functions"! This means that the answers to the question before and after November 17th are not directly comparable.

 From October 19, 2026, they ask about Super Intelligence

 When I went looking for the updated question language in the latest XLSX file, I couldn't find it. I found this instead:

 In the last two weeks, did this business use Super Intelligence or SI (formerly referred to as Artificial Intelligence or AI) in any of its business functions? (Examples of SI use include: SI-powered data analysis; generative SI for marketing, product design, or coding; virtual SI agents for customer service; SI-powered forecasting or pricing; SI-driven computer vision for quality control, etc.)

 The BTOS about page explains what happened:

 Beginning with the October 19, 2026 collection, instrument wording was updated due to Executive Order 14434 .

 The current numbers reflect the old Artificial Intelligence survey wording - the first survey results reflecting the Super Intelligence wording are due for publication on Thursday.

 Is this going to affect the survey?

 The obvious open question here is whether this wording change is going to affect the survey results.

 The businesses answering this survey will have last seen that question twelve weeks ago, when it was still called AI. Hopefully the new language isn't going to confuse them, especially since the survey helpfully spells out "formerly referred to as Artificial Intelligence or AI".

 I can't help but laugh at the absurdity of "SI-powered data analysis; generative SI for marketing, product design, or coding; virtual SI agents for customer service" though.

 Tags: census , surveys , ai , generative-ai , llms

blogs.name: Import AI
blogs.title: Import AI 479: Spacewar; low-latency tasks versus LLMs; Genie 4
blogs.author: Jack Clark
blogs.description: Welcome to Import AI, a newsletter about AI research. Import AI runs on arXiv, cappuccinos, and feedback from readers. If you’d like to…
blogs.content:
Welcome to Import AI, a newsletter about AI research. Import AI runs on arXiv, cappuccinos, and feedback from readers. If you’d like to support this, please subscribe.

 Subscribe now

 LLMs are very bad at low-latency tasks:
 …Realtime-Bench says it’ll be a while till AI systems can play games or do online auctions for you…
 Researchers have built Realtime-Bench, “a suite of carefully curated dynamic tasks where delayed actions directly affect success”. The test helps evaluate how well modern, general-purpose AI systems can perform tasks where decisions need to be made in real-time.
 The benchmark consists of 50 interactive game and web tasks, split across 30 web tasks in four categories (travel, e-commerce, service, and security), and 20 game tasks (arcade, puzzle, strategy, and simulation).

 Who did the research: The benchmark was built by people at the University of Texas at Austin, Ohio State University, University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign, NVIDIA, Northwestern University, and Steadyworks.

 What it measures: The test is designed to probe for three qualities: temporal state awareness (”RT-Perceive”), where models can use observations to track changes in the world; adaptive deliberation (”RT-Deliberate”), where models alter their reasoning length and depth according to available time; and time-aware action selection (”RT-Act”) where models need to appropriately time their actions for the situation.
 “For example, an agent purchasing a ticket must track the sale status and assess whether observed availability is still current (RT-Perceive), limit further deliberation when the purchase window is closing (RT-Deliberate), and choose between waiting for sales to open and purchasing while tickets remain available (RT-Act).”
 They have three different conditions: Wall clock, which is designed to test out performance under real-world latency. Paused clock, which lets you arbitrarily pause things so you can get a sense of baseline capability, and Token clock, which “advances the environment at a fixed rate per generation token. An action is applied at the simulated time reached when it is committed, so consuming more tokens delays execution regardless of actual inference latency”.

 How well do models do? The authors tested out models from OpenAI (GPT-6-Astra, GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-Realtime-2, OpenAI Decisions), Anthropic (Claude Fable 5.1, Claude Opus 5), Google (Gemini 3.8 Flash, Gemini 3.1 Flash Live, Gemini 3.8 Live), Jev 1.13, as well as Chinese models from Deepseek (V4.1) and Moonshot AI (Kimi-K3).
 GPT-6 Astra (high) got the highest pass rate on the ‘wall clock’ evaluation setting, with 36%.
 By comparison, with a paused clock, models with high reasoning get closer to 70% or even 80% success.

 Why this matters: This benchmark is an effective proxy for where AI agents will break – the low scores here point to tasks where AI agents cannot yet be expected to perform well.
 Check out the leaderboard : Realtime-Bench (official website) .
 Read the paper : Realtime-Bench: Can Frontier Models Solve Real-time Interactive Problems? (arXiv) .

 ***

 The future of spacewar, courtesy of the Defense Intelligence Agency:
 …Anti-satellite tech, space nukes, and more…
 Working in AI can be stressful so sometimes to relax myself I like to read about other topics to get a sense for what horrors lie elsewhere. I take the same approach with depression, where if I feel sad I will try and listen to music by people sadder than me in an attempt to cheer myself up (e.g., Radiohead, Neil Young, and in very dark moments Bill Callahan / Smog, etc).
 So with that in mind I recently read “Challenges to Security in Space”, by the Defense Intelligence Agency.

 What’s going on in space: As with conflict on Earth, space is defined by conflict between the US versus China, Russia, Iran, and North Korea, with China the most technologically sophisticated, and Russia the most seemingly gung ho.
 “China and Russia are developing a formidable spectrum of offensive capabilities to degrade or destroy space services of other countries, from kinetic destruction to sophisticated jamming and cyber operations,” the DIA writes. “China has more than tripled its space launches per year in the past decade, with 22 launches in 2016 and 93 launches in 2025… Beijing judges space is central to the United States and its allies’ operations. Beijing also considers space an offensive military domain, which has shaped integral components of PLA military planning and campaigns.”

 Spacewar: The general vibe you get from reading this 100+ page report is there is a huge amount of ugly, frightening stuff happening in space, or being done to things in space by things on the ground. Some example quotes:

 “By the late 2020s, China may field space-based directed energy systems and higher-powered ground-based directed energy systems capable of threatening satellites in higher orbits”

 “China is developing space-based technology, including on-orbit counterspace weapons, capable of holding space systems at risk”

 “Russia’s Peresvet, a ground-based laser system, is designed to dazzle enemy satellites’ optical systems to mask the movement of Russia’s strategic missile systems”

 “Russia has launched several satellites over the last few years which conducted test activities on orbit for technologies that could enable attacks on other countries’ satellites and result in temporary or permanent damage”

 China has a couple of spaceplanes, akin to the US’s hyper-secret X-37B vehicle, and they appear to be getting more sophisticated. In 2023, one of China’s aforementioned vehicles, “released and interacted with an object.”

 Satellite-on-satellite fights: It’s obvious throughout the report that we’re in a world where rival nations have satellites that try to go up and mess with other satellites from other people.

 “In 2019, Russia launched satellite Cosmos 2542, which released a second satellite, Cosmos 2543. Cosmos 2543 then began following a U.S. national security satellite and approached it multiple times at a distance close enough to create potentially dangerous operating conditions,” the DIA writes. “Russia is developing kinetic orbital systems to permanently disable, or “kill,” satellites. Moscow’s Burevestnik is a developmental, co-orbital air-launched ASAT weapon for killing spacecraft in LEO”.

 “In February 2022, Russia launched a satellite called Cosmos, which Moscow claimed at the time was testing the effects of space radiation on electronic systems. This satellite was launched into an unusual and isolated orbit not used by any other spacecraft”.

 Space nukes: Russia is experimenting with nukes in space. “A nuclear detonation in space would create an electromagnetic pulse, which would immediately affect satellites within range and could impact civilian infrastructure,” the DIA writes. “A nuclear detonation in space could be tailored to impact satellites in most orbits—LEO for commercial and reconnaissance satellites, GEO for critical communications, and MEO for navigation and timing satellites”.

 Why this matters – infrastructure for the next phase of the AI power struggle: As people spend more resources on building space-based data centers (and eventually, perhaps, lunar-based ones), space will become ever more strategically and commercially valuable and ever more contested. Research like this gives us a sense of the hardware which is already in space and will arrive in the future. Perhaps in some far-off future an AI might seek to take control of such space assets as well.
 Read more: DIA Releases Challenges to Security in Space (Defense Intelligence Agency, press release) .
 Read the report : Challenges to Security in Space (DIA, PDF) .

 ***

 Metis: A startup trying to fuse symbolic and neural reasoning:
 …Towards Vulcan-like machine minds…
 Metis, a startup that wants to build novel AI architectures oriented around developing machines with better reasoning, has published a research paper laying out its research approach. The high-level summary is simple – Metis wants to do for modern open-domain problems what DeepMind did for closed-domain problems like board games via its work on AlphaGo and AlphaGo Zero.

 What they want to do: The key idea here is to add a reasoning core to modern AI architectures which is far more reliable than what we have today. “In modern AI architectures much of the other surrounding machinery that made AlphaGo a successful reasoning system remains either implicit or absent,” they write. “The first missing element is an explicit and persistent epistemic state… the second missing element is a criterion that allows the system to choose reasoning moves that make progress towards the goal.”
 This is more of a position paper than a technical paper, so they don’t have a ton of detail here. The main idea is to train a reasoning policy and value function based on real-world data collection, then use this to guide the system to perform reasoning that reduces long-term uncertainty, and have these sit on a basic core of data made up of claims or hypotheses about the world. “Any change to a claim’s evidential status must be licensed by evidence or verified through explicit calculation and approved by an independent judgment system,” they write. “Model-generated content cannot enter the accepted epistemic state merely by being plausible; it must pass warrant assessment, which lowers hallucinations. Sources of evidence can be attached directly to the propositions they support, providing a clear chain of provenance. The reasoning process becomes explicitly auditable.”

 Why this matters – building reliable substrates that are also deeply inhuman: Ideas like the architecture described here are fascinating both because of the promise they bring for increasing the reliability of AI systems, but also for how deeply inhuman they are: humans do not reason from some pristine base of facts, rather it’s all a big messy blob of memory and intuitions and some rules (some of which are learned from experience and some of which seem more platonic, like forms of logical reasoning). In this way, contemporary LLMs are more like humans than the system described here.
 “While the history of AI can be understood as a contest between symbolic and neural methods, it may be more constructive to view it as a story of two incomplete successes,” Metis writes. “Classical systems made aspects of the reasoning process explicit but depended on representations, operators, heuristics and knowledge supplied largely by hand. Contemporary LLMs learn extraordinary semantic operations and vast bodies of implicit knowledge but leave the organisation, evaluation and accumulation of reasoning implicit.”
 The AI system described here would ‘think’ in a way that is very different to how humans think and such a system might show us more about the differences between our own intelligence and that of machines.
 Read more: The Age of Reasoning (Metis, PDF) .

 ***

 Google summons Genie 4 for better world modeling:
 …One of Google’s most interesting projects continues to live!…
 Google DeepMind has published details on Genie 4, a new iteration of its Genie world model. The company is rolling out access to Genie 4 currently as a research preview for some trusted testers and will eventually come to Google AI Ultra subscribers. The Genie series of models are fascinating, showing a world where you can take a photograph of anything and turn it into an interactable environment, or one where you can convert a 2D drawing into the stage for a videogame, and more.

 Key features: Google calls out four features that make Genie 4 different to previous ones. These include:

 Real-time modification : “You can use natural language to modify a simulation in real-time — like changing the weather, moving the camera, or introducing a new person or object — and Gemini will contextually adapt your prompt to match the surrounding scene.”

 Physics and human action simulatio...

 Good morning, {{ first_name | AI enthusiasts }}, and welcome to our 8,118 new readers. AI spent the last two years winning over Washington. This week, it faces a tougher crowd: voters ready to hit the polls and evict the buildout from their own backyards.
 With data centers now a defining midterm issue, OpenAI already floating a new name for them, and control of the House up for grabs, AI’s next wave of construction could get a lot harder — no matter what the industry decides to call it.

---

 Data centers hit the ballot as OpenAI plots a rebrand

 Make AI artwork you can actually edit

 LATEST DEVELOPMENTS

 AI & POLITICS
 🗳️ Data centers hit the ballot as OpenAI plots a rebrand
 Image source: Wikimedia Commons

 The Rundown: This week’s U.S. midterms double as a referendum on data centers, with roughly 20 communities voting on bans or pauses, while OpenAI reportedly prepares a post-election push to rebrand the sites as “AI compute campuses.”
 The details:
 Democrats are projected to flip the House Tuesday, which could end a two-year run of easy treatment in Washington for AI firms with close ties to Pres. Trump.

 Some Democrats want a federal freeze on new data centers, including House hopefuls Will Lawrence in Michigan and Rebecca Cooke in Wisconsin.

 The White House already got tech giants to voluntarily supply their own power, and last week Trump floated having developers pay locals a “dividend” as well.

 OpenAI is planning to pitch the campuses as local economic boosts, citing a Pike County, Ohio, project it’s helping build that promises thousands of jobs.

 OpenAI policy chief Chris Lehane called the debate “democracy in action,” and the company wants state bills giving locals a voice in new projects.

 Why it matters: AI has a real image problem with the public, and data centers have become one of the defining fights of Tuesday’s elections. That anger won’t be fixed by a new name or a few community perks, and a Democratic House could make life a lot harder for AI giants trying to scale their infrastructure bets against local opposition.

 TOGETHER WITH GARTNER
 📓  Is your AI strategy ready for what’s next?  

 The Rundown: 42% of enterprises plan to deploy AI agents by the end of 2026, but only 22% capture significant value today. The Gartner Top Tech Trends for 2027 reveal how enterprises can shift into the autonomous era and get ahead.
 Key themes include:
 Leveraging the nontextual AI frontier

 Governing the autonomous agent platform

 Architecting durable agility

 Explore the trends .

 THE RUNDOWN ROUNDTABLE
 💡  The Rundown Roundtable: Our AI use cases

 The Rundown: The Rundown Roundtable is a weekly feature where we poll members of The Rundown staff about how we use AI in our work and daily lives.
 Nick, Video Producer:   When I create video content, I pull imagery from many different sources, so my editing folder often ends up with photos that may or may not work inside my editing program. For a handful of photos, converting them manually is fine. For larger projects with dozens of images, it eats into my time and focus. I wanted something simple, lightweight on compute power, that could batch convert photos.
 I asked Claude to create an app that runs on my local machine and can batch convert photos into formats I know will work in my video editor.
 Claude returned an app that worked exactly the way I needed. I asked Claude to install it on my computer, and it was working within seconds. I now use the app to batch convert my photo folders before bringing them into the editor.
 There are plenty of traditional ways to do this, but with Claude I got a solution that fit my workflow perfectly, and large image batches no longer slow my editing down.
 Shubham, Editor: I had about $2K in contributions from past jobs stuck in a government scheme for more than two years. The portal was slow, spread across several forms, and unclear about how to withdraw the money.
 I gave the task to Claude and Perplexity Comet. Claude worked through the rules and found the withdrawal route that kept my tax bill lowest. Comet then verified and implemented that route. It ran the portal in my browser, filled in and submitted the claim forms, and let me watch the screen and check each detail before submission. Two weeks later, the $2K arrived.
 After that, Claude compared the amount I received with the scheme’s online statement and found a gap: interest that had not been paid out. It filed a second form for the difference, and I’m waiting for the payment now. I’ll use the same technique to solve this for my wife, too.

 AI TRAINING
 🎨   Make AI artwork you can actually edit

 The Rundown: In this guide, you’ll use Arrow 2 to create a three-part graphic for a client proposal. You’ll refine one scene, add editable headings, and change a color without generating the artwork again.
 Step-by-step:
 Open QuiverAI, select Arrow 2, and check that your plan includes SVG export. Install Inkscape for the final text and color changes

 Paste the guide’s brief to draw a folder, review board, and laptop in one matching style. Leave space for the title and headings

 Ask Arrow to replace one badge with speech bubbles. Compare the result with the original and check that the other scenes stay intact

 Download the SVG and open it in Inkscape. Add the headings, then change the middle label and one screen color directly

 Save the editable master and export a high-resolution PNG. Reopen both files and check the words, colors, and dimensions before sharing

 Pro tip: Keep text that may change in separate text boxes. You can fix a heading or update a client’s wording without spending another generation on the artwork. Visit The Rundown University to get the full guide, materials, files, and more.

 PRESENTED BY CONDUCTOR
 🔎  Discover your brand’s top AEO priority

 The Rundown: Trade chance for certainty with Conductor’s free AEO Analysis. Compare your mentions with competitors, see which content gets cited, understand funnel visibility, and identify opportunities. 500+ brands are already winning AI search with Conductor.
 The free report analyzes:
 AI market share showing your brand mentions vs. competitors

 Funnel visibility with top prompts by search intent

 Content performance based on total AI citations

 Brand sentiment revealing how AI perceives your brand

 Get your free AEO analysis .

 AI, DATACENTERS, & SPACE
 🛰️ Google’s space data center sends home a haiku
 Image source: Google / SpaceX

 The Rundown: Google   just announced that its Project Suncatcher satellite answered its first AI prompt from orbit, with Google’s open Gemma 4 model writing a haiku in an early test of the company’s moonshot goal to put AI data centers in space.
 The details:
 Gemma’s haiku (Blue marble below / Data streams in silent grace / Starlight feeds my core) reached the ground while the satellite passed over Svalbard, Norway.

 Google CEO Sundar Pichai called it “a ‘hello world’ milestone,” a reference to the test programmers typically run first on a new machine.

 Power is still a big constraint, with the craft able to run just one of its four Google AI chips (TPUs), and only in bursts of roughly 20 minutes.

 Two more powerful satellites launching in 2027 will test the laser links a fleet needs to split one AI job, if the chips first survive radiation and heat tests.

 Why it matters: An admittedly heartwarming haiku still won’t win over a public that is increasingly fed up with data centers of any kind, but moving them to orbit could eventually be a compromise that sidesteps a lot of the issues driving that anger — making this moonshot project a big one to keep an eye on.

 QUICK HITS

 COMMUNITY AI WORKFLOW OF THE DAY
 ▸ John built an AI ops team for his photography business
 Today’s workflow comes from reader John Fertic :
 “I run a photography business and built a three-layer AI workflow to help with daily operations, business improvement, and watching for outside changes that might affect us. It's for small business owners who don't want to monitor every source or handle every issue themselves.
 The layers are an Operations Core (dashboard, estimates, schedules, reminders, project records, and other business state), a Work orchestrator with specialist AI agents, and a signal and triage system that watches platform alerts, vendor updates, local-search changes, newsletters, calendars, and marketing sources.
 Work decides whether a signal actually matters and routes it to the right specialist. The WordPress and Google Business Profile specialists are connected directly to those systems through MCP/API connectors, so they can compare the incoming signal against the current state of the actual site or profile. The system brings me in only when a real decision is needed. The main benefit for me is that I don't have to personally track every source or jump into every issue.”

There are 4 layers in the AI stack, each with a fundamental question before it.

 Application

 Breakout hits appear overnight. The next model release can erase them just as fast. Thin wrappers die when the model absorbs their feature. To build a moat, app companies must decide whether to build a brand, disrupt incumbents through pricing, develop their own models, or expand faster than competitors.

 Agents do the work with headless software. Will a user interface survive, or do all applications collapse into middleware harnesses 1 ?

 Harness & Context

 If applications collapse into middleware, the fight moves to who owns the harness. Model makers claim their native harness wins. The benchmarks say otherwise. In the same week, both OpenAI & Anthropic models scored higher in Cursor than in their creators’ own harnesses 2 . Because input context is up to 98% of all tokens 2 , a smart harness cuts the cost of the same answer by 71% & lifts gross margin from 38% to 75% 3 .

 Beyond the model makers, enterprises are starting to lay claim to the harness to build corporate sovereign AI 4 . No CIO wants to ship company secrets out the door in a prompt. Owning the context layer lets a company keep its memory & permissions in house while swapping models underneath.

 Model

 For foundation models, the question is at what point training costs don’t pay back. Training a state-of-the-art model costs billions 5 . Recursive self-improvement, AI models training better AI, has not yet bailed out the big labs. AI writes 75% of Google DeepMind’s production code, yet Google sees no end-to-end speedup in AI research 6 .

 On the demand side, Rich Sutton’s Bitter Lesson argues that general models scaled with massive compute always win 7 . Yet SOTA models are losing token share on public gateways because they cost too much to run 8 . About 83% of agent tasks now route to smaller or domain-specific models fine-tuned to do one job for a fraction of the bill 9 .

 Challengers are attacking the training bill through process & architecture. One startup used coding agents to pre-train a competitive coding model with a single researcher for under $10m 10 . New architectures like diffusion models 11 & JEPA, where a 109m model beat 72b LLMs with 42x less data 12 , bypass brute-force scaling.

 Still, the bull case for scaling the frontier sits in Anthropic’s S-1. Opus 5.5 cut customer cost per task by 40%, & when Opus 4.5 delivered more capability at a lower cost per task than Opus 4.1, Jevons paradox kicked in & sequential quarterly revenue growth accelerated from 48% to 132% 13 .

 Data Center

 Below the models, the question is whether credit & power can keep up with GPU demand. With concrete prices up 3x, electrical grids strained, & backlogs on turbines, generators, & reciprocating engines, the answer for now is no 14 .

 Unrestrained growth in AI requires $4t in new debt over five years, making the AI credit market larger than global private credit & equal to 91% of the US municipal bond market 15 . Are there enough lenders left at attractive rates? Risk strains insurance costs. Five-year credit default swap spreads have hit records from Meta (108 bps) to Oracle (322 bps) & CoreWeave (1,090 bps) 16 .

 On the ground, local politics & grid delays are blocking new sites, while Ornn’s B300 index has climbed to $12.29 per GPU-hour (~20% CMGR since June) 17 .

 Meanwhile, three open questions hang over the math : whether cash flows match the duration of twenty-year debt & leases 15 , whether GPUs last five years, & whether the price of a GPU-hour will increase or decrease 18 .

 How the Layers Interplay

 None of these four questions stands alone. Applications that generate tremendous profits at the top can sustain inflation in GPU prices & higher borrowing costs at the bottom. New, more efficient architectures 19 can decrease the need for concrete & copper. Surging GPU prices can swing the economics of the whole stack.

 Like a double pendulum 20 , the four layers form a coupled system : simple in each part, yet complex, chaotic, & unpredictable in motion.
